standardMappings.verificationUse: Build a converging workload/performance package covering accuracy, time, cognitive processing, communication, errors, and mission/task performance.
standardMappings.caveat: A questionnaire alone does not demonstrate acceptable workload. Confirm invocation, tailoring, user population, task, and acceptance criteria.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Use calibrated luminance, contrast, uniformity, and reflection measurements under the clause-specific geometry and ambient conditions.
standardMappings.caveat: Preserve each number with its exact subsection, units, geometry, ambient condition, uncertainty, and tailoring status; task readability remains separate evidence.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Evaluate outside-view compatibility, information limitation, eye box, angular displacement, character/symbol geometry, luminance, line width, and viewing accommodation.
standardMappings.caveat: The criterion and test condition—not the generic measure name—determine pass/fail. Confirm whether the implementation is a HUD, HMD, or other display.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Build HMD evidence around mission-derived FOV/FOR, symbology, clutter, cognitive load, real-world/control access, grayscale, depth, fit, stability, head movement, balance, and neck fatigue.
standardMappings.caveat: No single HMD score verifies this bundle. Separate optical/engineering measures, representative-user task evidence, and physical-ergonomic evidence.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Demonstrate population accommodation with appropriate univariate and multivariate boundary cases across simultaneous reach, clearance, vision, restraint, and control constraints.
standardMappings.caveat: Percentile manikins do not establish multivariate accommodation. Record the approved population model, equipment, posture, boundary cases, and failed constraints.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Measure system transport delay, HMD latency, flicker, refresh/update, fast-stimulus presentation, sickness contributors, and task/decision/workload fidelity.
standardMappings.caveat: Simulator fidelity is claim-specific. A local visual or latency test does not establish transfer to flight or operational effectiveness.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Demonstrate display/control readability from design eye points in bright full sun up to 10,000 fc, night/dark conditions, and lighting extremes with representative helmet/visor equipment.
standardMappings.caveat: 516D is guidance and the certification authority selects/tailors the criterion and method. Do not label the system “516D compliant.”

standardMappings.verificationUse: Use design-eye analysis plus representative-user/equipment mockup or aircraft evidence for interior/exterior visibility, reach, clearance, seats, restraints, and controls.
standardMappings.caveat: State the intended anthropometric population, production-representative geometry, equipment, task set, and authority-approved acceptance criteria.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Assess alert perception, recognition, discrimination, legibility, and correct action under concurrent stimuli, lighting, optical gear, cascading failures, and representative stressors.
standardMappings.caveat: The program certification basis controls. A detection score without diagnosis/action and scenario conditions is incomplete evidence.

standardMappings.locator: §§9.4.1–9.4.6; public PDF pp. 548–549 and following criteria
standardMappings.verificationUse: Combine functional/task analysis, workload including situation awareness, objective speed/accuracy/heading, HITL simulation, flight test, unusual-attitude recovery, external vision, error handling, and automation evidence.
standardMappings.caveat: Select measures against the approved certification criterion and mission-task element. Supporting scales do not replace objective task performance or authority judgment.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Assess installed communications intelligibility using listener testing such as the Modified Rhyme Test and STIPA only where technically valid.
standardMappings.caveat: STIPA is not valid for every processed/encoded communications chain. Preserve the complete signal path, noise, equipment, language, hearing, and test-method suitability.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Trace sensory, cognitive, physiological, timing, effort, stress, normal/emergency/degraded tasks, representative users, quantitative criteria, discrepancies, and error causes.
standardMappings.caveat: Invoked and tailored program requirements control. The standard requires a defensible HE process, not a universal named scale.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Plan calibrated display/HUD/HMD tests for resolution, legibility, color, NVIS, flicker, jitter, noise, reflection, solar effects, latency, geometry, and optical performance.
standardMappings.caveat: Guidance only. Sample specification paragraphs include blanks and unresolved text; use the program requirement for acceptance values.

standardMappings.locator: Applicable NVIS radiance, chromaticity, lighting, control, and display clauses; verify equipment class/type
standardMappings.verificationUse: Measure NVIS-weighted radiance and chromaticity and demonstrate readable, compatible lighting/display operation in the installed NVIS configuration.
standardMappings.caveat: Use the exact invoked revision, equipment class/type, clause, source state, spectral method, and test geometry. General legibility remains separate evidence.

standardMappings.locator: Appendix B and Appendix C.1/C.6; report pp. 354–356, 364–365, 381–387
standardMappings.verificationUse: Pair objective task time, steps, accuracy, errors, and recovery with relevant subjective, display, control, workload, comfort, and observer evidence in representative scenarios.
standardMappings.caveat: Reference guidance, not an automatic means of compliance. Preference can diverge from performance, and people do not reliably estimate their own times or errors.

standardMappings.verificationUse: Provides explicit HITL/task, time/accuracy, usability, error, Bedford workload, Borg CR10, SAGAT/SART, legibility, latency, brightness, contrast, gamut, glare, reflection, vibration, and position benchmarks for human spaceflight.
standardMappings.caveat: Not automatically applicable to aircraft or military airworthiness. Use only when invoked or label clearly as supplemental context.

standardMappings.locator: Public ASSIST scope/status only; full B text controlled
standardMappings.verificationUse: Flags handling-qualities candidates that may support an approved MIL-STD-1797B program basis after authorized clause review.
standardMappings.caveat: No clause-level mapping is asserted from the public record. Obtain authorized text and the program certification/test basis before use.

studies.title: NASA Task Load Index (TLX): Paper and Pencil Package, Version 1.0
studies.use: Documents the six dimension ratings and original pairwise-weighting procedure; reports development across more than 40 laboratory, simulation, and in-flight experiments.
studies.context: Workload measurement program spanning laboratory, simulation, and flight contexts.
studies.appraisal: Use the original instructions for the selected TLX version and record whether pairwise weighting is performed. Development breadth is not a universal reliability coefficient.

studies.title: Development of NASA-TLX: Results of Empirical and Theoretical Research
studies.use: Presents the conceptual and empirical basis for the multidimensional TLX and its weighting procedure.
studies.context: Workload experiments used to develop a multidimensional subjective assessment method.
studies.appraisal: Strong identity and development source; it does not make every later modified or raw administration equivalent to the original procedure.

studies.title: Psychometric Properties of Subjective Workload Measurement Techniques
studies.use: Compared the measurement properties and differing psychometric structures of NASA-TLX and SWAT.
studies.context: Subjective workload-measure comparison.
studies.appraisal: Useful evidence that scale structure changes what a measure is sensitive to; not a basis for treating TLX and SWAT as interchangeable.

studies.title: Comparison of Four Subjective Workload Rating Scales
studies.use: Compared TLX, SWAT, Modified Cooper–Harper, and Overall Workload across five studies involving three U.S. Army systems.
studies.context: Five studies and three Army systems with subjective workload ratings.
studies.appraisal: All four scales were sensitive to workload levels in these studies; TLX and Overall Workload were stronger on the reported factor-validity and operator-acceptance comparisons. Do not generalize beyond the tested systems without local evidence.

studies.title: The Effects of Perceptual-Motor Task Difficulty on Subjective Workload
studies.use: Used NASA-TLX and SWAT after tracking trials manipulating control order, feedback, and input device.
studies.context: Controlled perceptual-motor tracking experiment.
studies.appraisal: Perceived-workload patterns mirrored several performance effects and the two scales had equivalent sensitivity in this experiment; that does not establish universal equivalence.

studies.title: NASA-TLX; 20 Years Later
studies.use: Reviews two decades of NASA-TLX use and modifications.
studies.context: Retrospective review across application areas.
studies.appraisal: Useful for adoption and modification history; it is not a new universal reliability or validity study.

studies.title: Evaluation of Mental Workload in Simulator and Flight Test
studies.use: Compared workload in simulator and flight-test conditions using NASA-TLX.
studies.context: Simulator-to-flight workload comparison.
studies.appraisal: The reported simulator-to-flight TLX correlation is context-specific cross-setting evidence; it does not establish that simulator TLX always predicts in-flight workload.

studies.title: What Does a Post-Run NASA-TLX Rating Summarize?
studies.use: Compared post-run NASA-TLX with retrospective minute-by-minute ratings after a contrived flight-simulator scenario.
studies.context: Flight simulation with temporally varying workload.
studies.appraisal: Directly relevant to the temporal meaning of post-run ratings; retain scenario construction and retrospective-rating limitations.

studies.title: An Empirical Evaluation of the System Usability Scale
studies.use: Analyzed 2,324 questionnaires from 206 studies across product types and examined score distribution, reliability, and component structure.
studies.context: Large mixed-product usability-study archive.
studies.appraisal: The reported alpha and one-component pattern belong to this product/test mix. They are not guaranteed for an aviation population or modified scale.

studies.title: The Factor Structure of the System Usability Scale
studies.use: Analyzed independent datasets and proposed Usable (items 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) and Learnable (items 4, 10) components.
studies.context: Reanalysis plus an independent archive of SUS responses from usability tests.
studies.appraisal: Supports investigating dimensionality; the two-item Learnable score is less stable and later research has not made the factor solution universal. Preserve the total-score interpretation unless the subscore use is justified.

studies.title: On the Dimensionality of the System Usability Scale: a Test of Alternative Measurement Models
studies.use: Compared one-factor, uncorrelated two-factor, and correlated two-factor CFA models and reported standardized item loadings for the preferred correlated model.
studies.context: 196 university users evaluating one Italian website; maximum-likelihood CFA.
studies.appraisal: The correlated two-factor model fit this sample better, but the single system and student population limit transfer. The stored item loadings are study-specific evidence, not permanent item properties.

studies.title: Psychometric Evaluation of an After-Scenario Questionnaire for Computer Usability Studies
studies.use: Used a three-item after-scenario questionnaire across three usability tests with eight common scenarios.
studies.context: Scenario-level computer usability tests.
studies.appraisal: Supports scenario-specific ease/satisfaction measurement under the studied conditions. ASQ should not replace objective completion/error evidence or a post-study overall measure.

studies.title: IBM Computer Usability Satisfaction Questionnaires: Psychometric Evaluation and Instructions for Use
studies.use: Reports ASQ, PSSUQ, and CSUQ scoring, internal-consistency evidence, and three named PSSUQ/CSUQ factors.
studies.context: IBM usability studies, including a preliminary 48-person PSSUQ factor analysis and a 377-response CSUQ study.
studies.appraisal: A key instrument source. Reported coefficients and factor results are tied to these datasets and versions; aviation transfer and any wording changes require new evidence.

studies.title: UMUX-LITE: When There’s No Time for the SUS
studies.use: Developed a two-item usefulness/ease measure and compared it with SUS in two studies.
studies.context: Usability evaluations of products/systems in two samples.
studies.appraisal: Efficient for a narrow perceived-usability construct; with only two items, do not report alpha or claim diagnostic coverage of usability, safety, workload, or legibility.

studies.title: Situational Awareness Rating Technique: The Development of a Tool for Aircrew Systems Design
studies.use: Developed SART using structured knowledge elicitation with 84 RAF test and operational aircrew; used principal-components analysis and clustering to organize ten dimensions.
studies.context: Aircrew systems design and aviation situation-awareness judgments.
studies.appraisal: Strong domain-origin evidence, but SART is subjective perceived SA. The 10D and 3D forms/scoring are not interchangeable without naming the version.

studies.title: Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART): The Evaluation of an Airborne Display System
studies.use: Compared 10-dimensional and 3-dimensional SART with NASA-TLX in a computer-graphics flight-simulation evaluation.
studies.context: Twelve RAF pilots in flight simulation.
studies.appraisal: Relevant aviation application, but the small specialist sample and shared subjective method require objective task companions and cautious generalization.

studies.title: A Comparative Analysis of SAGAT and SART for Evaluations of Situation Awareness
studies.use: Compared subjective SART and freeze-probe SAGAT in a display evaluation.
studies.context: Display evaluation with situation-awareness manipulations.
studies.appraisal: Both were sensitive/diagnostic in the study, but were not correlated; SART aligned with confidence and subjective performance. Do not treat SART and SAGAT as interchangeable.

studies.title: An Efficient Screening Technique for Acceptable Mental Workload Based on the NASA Task Load Index—Development and Application to Control Room Validation
studies.use: Collected NASA-TLX and three-item SART after sessions and video review across 12 control-room scenarios.
studies.context: Eighteen licensed operators working as six three-person teams.
studies.appraisal: The source reported reliability estimates but found no clear evidence that the SART index measured situation awareness in that setting. Repeated team/scenario ratings are not independent observations.

studies.title: Flight Evaluation of a Head-Worn Display for Low-Visibility Operations
studies.use: Administered three-dimensional SART after taxi and approach trials alongside workload, flight technical error, and display-attribute ratings.
studies.context: NASA head-worn-display flight test for low-visibility operations.
studies.appraisal: Good triangulation pattern because subjective SA was not the only endpoint. Device, task, crew, and operational context limit transfer.

studies.title: Measurement of Situation Awareness in Dynamic Systems
studies.use: Describes freeze-probe measurement, requirements-derived queries, scoring, and evidence concerning intrusion and validity.
studies.context: Dynamic human–machine systems including aviation-relevant tasks.
studies.appraisal: Queries must come from a task/goal analysis and synchronized ground truth. A generic quiz or confidence rating is not SAGAT.

studies.title: Direct Measurement of Situation Awareness: Validity and Use of SAGAT
studies.use: Compared SAGAT, SART, and objective performance under manipulations intended to affect pilot situation awareness.
studies.context: Rotorcraft simulation/aviation situation-awareness evaluation.
studies.appraisal: Directly useful comparison evidence; preserve manipulation, task, probe, and simulator details before transferring a result.

studies.title: A Subjective Rating Scale for Assessing Pilot Workload in Flight: A Decade of Practical Use
studies.use: Describes the ten-point decision-tree scale based on spare mental capacity and reports flight-trial use with pilots.
studies.context: Pilot workload assessment in defined flight tasks.
studies.appraisal: Appropriate for pilot spare-capacity judgments when the exact decision tree and training are used. Do not treat it as a generic satisfaction scale.

studies.title: Human Factors Evaluation of a Head-Up Display in Degraded Visual Conditions
studies.use: Administered Bedford immediately after simulated rotary-wing approach and landing phases during a HUD evaluation.
studies.context: Rotary-wing simulator, degraded visual conditions, phase-specific ratings.
studies.appraisal: The phase-linked timing is defensible. Generalization depends on the display, flight task, pilot population, and simulator fidelity; pair ratings with achieved performance.

studies.title: The Use of Pilot Rating in the Evaluation of Aircraft Handling Qualities
studies.use: Defines the handling-qualities decision tree, required pilot compensation, and desired/adequate task-performance logic.
studies.context: Piloted-aircraft handling-qualities evaluation.
studies.appraisal: Use only for a specified task, configuration, criteria, and trained pilot judgment. It is ordinal handling-qualities evidence—not a general workload or usability scale.

studies.title: A Review of Pilot Rating Experience for Handling Qualities
studies.use: Reviews experience applying Cooper–Harper in aircraft and spacecraft handling-qualities work.
studies.context: Handling-qualities applications and interpretation.
studies.appraisal: Emphasizes ordinal, task/configuration-specific interpretation with pilot comments and task-performance data. It does not justify arithmetic treatment as an interval scale.

studies.title: Transport-Aircraft Rudder Control Evaluation
studies.use: Used Cooper–Harper after simulated transport-aircraft rudder maneuvers across combinations of pedal force, breakout force, and travel.
studies.context: Transport-aircraft simulation and rudder-control design variables.
studies.appraisal: Good example of coupling ratings to explicit control geometry/forces and a maneuver. It does not transfer a rating threshold to unrelated aircraft or tasks.

studies.title: Application of Conjoint Measurement to Workload Scale Development
studies.use: Reported development and tests of construct and concurrent validity for an early SWAT scale using conjoint measurement.
studies.context: Subjective workload scale development.
studies.appraisal: Important development evidence; users should follow the selected SWAT version and scaling procedure rather than treating three raw ratings as an arbitrary average.

studies.title: The Subjective Workload Assessment Technique: A Scaling Procedure for Measuring Mental Workload
studies.use: Defines time load, mental effort load, and psychological stress load plus the scale-development/event-scoring procedure.
studies.context: Mental workload assessment method.
studies.appraisal: Use the documented scaling/scoring approach and record individual or group solution. It is not interchangeable with TLX despite overlapping workload language.

studies.title: Subjective Workload Assessment Technique (SWAT): A User’s Guide
studies.use: Provides the public-release user guide for SWAT Version 3.1.
studies.context: Operational administration and scoring guidance.
studies.appraisal: Primary administration anchor; preserve version, sorting/scaling method, scoring solution, and task timing.

studies.title: ERGO Version 2: Instantaneous Self Assessment of Workload in a Real-Time Environment
studies.use: Documents a system for prompting and collecting ISA workload ratings during real-time air-traffic-control simulations.
studies.context: Real-time ATC simulation.
studies.appraisal: Supports synchronized momentary workload collection. Prompt frequency and response demand can alter the task, so reactivity must be assessed.

studies.title: An Experimental Evaluation of Instantaneous Self-Assessment as a Measure of Workload
studies.use: Compared ISA with post-task workload ratings, heart-rate measures, and tracking performance.
studies.context: Experimental tracking/workload task with manual and spoken prompts.
studies.appraisal: ISA was sensitive and correlated with several comparators, but primary tracking performance worsened whenever a response was required. Probe reactivity is a real validity threat.

studies.title: AMRUFRA Real-Time Validation
studies.use: Collected ISA every two minutes during exercises and NASA-TLX after each exercise.
studies.context: Real-time air-traffic-control validation exercises.
studies.appraisal: Useful example of keeping momentary and retrospective workload measures distinct. Repeated prompts, controller sample, and exercise design remain essential context.

studies.title: Evaluation of a Head-Worn Display System as an Equivalent Head-Up Display for Low Visibility Commercial Operations
studies.use: Combined flight technical performance, workload, SSQ, SART/SA-SWORD, comfort, optical/boresight/brightness/color/conformality/usability ratings, and attempted eye tracking.
studies.context: Low-visibility commercial-operations HWD/HUD-equivalence experiment.
studies.appraisal: A strong multi-method pattern. Eye tracking had roughly 70% bad gaze quality because the HWD obstructed the cameras—an explicit warning to verify sensor compatibility and data quality before relying on gaze results.

nasa-task-load-index-weighted.summary: Six-dimensional retrospective workload rating using the original pairwise weighting procedure.
nasa-task-load-index-weighted.administration: Rate six workload dimensions for each defined task segment, then obtain 15 pairwise source-of-workload choices after task exposure. Weight each dimension by its choice count and divide the weighted sum by 15.
administrationSteps: Define the participant, task or condition, and exact segment being rated. Use the same rating point across comparable conditions; collect the ratings during or soon after that segment, as specified in your protocol.

Explain the six dimensions below and their anchors to the participant. Resolve questions and allow practice before using scored ratings. Ask about the workload of the specified task, not general ability or the entire test day.

For every rated segment or condition, obtain all six dimension ratings on the original 0–100 scale in increments of 5. Record each rating separately. On the original paper scale, a mark between ticks is assigned to the tick on its right.

After the participant has experienced the task, present every distinct pair of the six dimension names once: 15 choices in a randomized order for each participant. For each pair ask which dimension contributed more to workload in that task. Use new weights for a structurally different task; document any reuse across comparable difficulty variants.
scoringSteps: For each participant and task structure, count how often each dimension was selected in the 15 pairs. Each weight is 0–5; the six weights must sum to 15.
For each rated task condition calculate (Mental×weight + Physical×weight + Temporal×weight + Performance×weight + Effort×weight + Frustration×weight) ÷ 15. The result is on a 0–100 scale.
Performance is anchored Good at the low end and Poor at the high end: a higher number means poorer perceived performance and more contribution to workload. Do not reverse-code it again.

Report the weighted composite together with the six ratings, six weights, task/segment and rating timing. State missing-rating or missing-pair handling; do not present an incomplete score as the original weighted TLX.

dimensionGuide.name: Mental Demand
dimensionGuide.meaning: Amount of thinking, deciding, remembering, looking and other mental or perceptual activity required.

dimensionGuide.name: Temporal Demand
dimensionGuide.meaning: Time pressure imposed by the pace of the task or its events.

dimensionGuide.name: Performance
dimensionGuide.meaning: The participant's perceived success at meeting the task goals.

dimensionGuide.name: Effort
dimensionGuide.meaning: Mental and physical work required to achieve that performance.

dimensionGuide.name: Frustration
dimensionGuide.meaning: Feeling insecure, discouraged, irritated or stressed rather than content and relaxed.

procedureSource.label: NASA-TLX Paper and Pencil Package, v1.0, §§2–4 and appendices A–E

nasa-task-load-index-weighted.licensing: NASA states that the TLX may be used or modified without seeking NASA permission. Preserve the original six dimensions and scoring if reporting the unmodified weighted TLX; identify and validate any adaptation.

reliabilityEvidence.label: No universal coefficient
reliabilityEvidence.result: TLX dimensions describe distinguishable workload contributors; a single internal-consistency coefficient is not sufficient evidence that every administration supports one reflective total score.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Protocol dependability
reliabilityEvidence.result: For repeated scenarios, evaluate within-person stability/condition discrimination and report the exact weighted scoring procedure and missing-data handling.
reliabilityEvidence.source: Repository synthesis grounded in the instrument structure

validityEvidence.label: Sensitivity and comparison
validityEvidence.result: Five-study Army comparison found all tested workload scales sensitive; TLX and Overall Workload were stronger on the reported factor-validity and operator-acceptance comparisons.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: A high TLX score does not alone establish unsafe workload, causal mechanism, or failure to meet a standard. Pair it with task performance, errors, conditions, and mechanism-relevant evidence.

factorEvidence.model: Multidimensional index; do not assume a reflective one-factor CFA
factorEvidence.estimator: Not represented here as one reusable CFA model
factorEvidence.result: Six rated workload dimensions with participant-specific weighting in the original procedure.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Analyze dimensions and total according to the prespecified estimand. A coefficient alpha across dimensions would not establish validity.

researchNeeds: Reliability/sensitivity in the intended pilot population

raw-nasa-tlx.summary: Unweighted mean or sum of the six NASA-TLX dimension ratings; a common modification that must be named as Raw TLX.
raw-nasa-tlx.administration: Rate the six NASA-TLX dimensions for each defined task segment and average the six ratings. Raw TLX deliberately omits the original pairwise weighting step.
administrationSteps: Define the participant, task or condition, and exact segment being rated. Use a consistent rating point across comparable conditions.
Explain the six dimensions below and their anchors; resolve questions and allow practice before scored ratings.

For every rated segment or condition, obtain all six ratings on the original 0–100 scale in increments of 5. Keep each dimension rating. On the original paper scale, a mark between ticks is assigned to the tick on its right.
Do not conduct the 15 pairwise comparisons when the intended result is Raw TLX. Name this unweighted variant explicitly in the protocol and report.
scoringSteps: For each participant and task condition, add the six dimension ratings and divide by 6: Raw TLX mean = Σ(six ratings) ÷ 6. This produces a 0–100 score.
Performance is anchored Good at the low end and Poor at the high end. A higher Performance rating means worse perceived performance; do not reverse-code it again.

Report the mean and all six dimension ratings, rating timing and task segment. If using a six-rating sum instead, label it explicitly as a 0–600 sum; do not compare its numeric level directly with 0–100 means or weighted TLX.
Do not label this result as the original weighted NASA-TLX or imply that published evidence for one scoring variant automatically validates the other.

dimensionGuide.meaning: Mental and physical work required to achieve that performance.
