raw-nasa-tlx.licensing: NASA states that the TLX may be used or modified without seeking NASA permission. Name Raw TLX as an unweighted variant and disclose any further item or response-scale changes.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Version-specific evidence needed
reliabilityEvidence.result: Do not transfer coefficients between weighted TLX, Raw TLX, altered scales, languages, populations, or task timing.

validityEvidence.label: Temporal interpretation
validityEvidence.result: A simulator study compared post-run TLX with retrospective minute-by-minute ratings to investigate what the summary represents.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: An unweighted total assumes an aggregation rule not used in the original weighted procedure. State and justify the change.

factorEvidence.estimator: Not a generic one-factor loading model
factorEvidence.result: Six conceptually distinct workload ratings are often retained and reported separately.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Do not use alpha alone to force dimensions into one latent factor. Evaluate the score interpretation for the intended task.

system-usability-scale-sus.summary: Ten-item post-use perceived-usability questionnaire scored as a 0–100 composite; it is not a percentage.
system-usability-scale-sus.administration: Administer all 10 items after representative use with the original five-point response format and alternating wording. Reverse-score the even items, sum item contributions, and multiply by 2.5. Do not interpret individual items alone.
system-usability-scale-sus.licensing: Use the original Brooke source and current instrument guidance; preserve wording and attribution and check permissions for translations or adaptations.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Large mixed-product archive
reliabilityEvidence.result: Bangor et al. reported coefficient alpha 0.911 for 2,324 questionnaires from 206 studies.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Proposed subscales
reliabilityEvidence.result: Lewis and Sauro reported alphas 0.91 for the eight-item Usable component and 0.70 for the two-item Learnable component in their source analysis.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Transfer warning
reliabilityEvidence.result: These coefficients describe their samples, versions, products, and scoring. Estimate reliability and uncertainty for the intended population and use.

validityEvidence.label: Known system differences and broad use
validityEvidence.result: The original item selection discriminated an easier from a harder system; later large archives support score interpretation across varied products.

validityEvidence.label: Internal-structure dispute
validityEvidence.result: One-component and correlated two-factor patterns have both been reported; subscore interpretation remains sample- and model-dependent.
validityEvidence.source: Bangor et al. (2008); Lewis & Sauro (2009); Borsci et al. (2009)

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: SUS measures perceived overall usability after use. It does not establish mission safety, readability, workload, objective efficiency, or compliance.
validityEvidence.source: Instrument construct and FAA evaluation guidance

factorEvidence.source: Borsci, Federici, & Lauriola (2009), Table 2 and Table 3
factorEvidence.sample: 196 university users evaluating one Italian website
factorEvidence.result: Correlated Usability and Learnability model fit better than the tested one-factor and uncorrelated two-factor models in this sample; factor correlation reported as 0.70.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Study-specific item evidence. Negative signs reflect item wording/coding in the reported solution. The single-system/student sample limits transfer.

factorEvidence.sample: Two independent SUS datasets; one archive contained 324 questionnaires from 19 tests
factorEvidence.estimator: Exploratory component/factor analyses reported by the authors
factorEvidence.result: Items 4 and 10 aligned with a Learnable component; the other eight aligned with a Usable component.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Supports checking dimensionality; does not make two subscores universally valid or independently diagnostic.

researchNeeds: Factor/model comparison for the exact version

after-scenario-questionnaire-asq.summary: Three-item scenario-level questionnaire covering ease of task completion, time, and support information.
after-scenario-questionnaire-asq.administration: Administer immediately after a defined scenario using the original item wording and response scale; retain item scores and link them to scenario performance.
after-scenario-questionnaire-asq.licensing: Use Lewis (1991/1995) as the administration and scoring anchor.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Scenario studies
reliabilityEvidence.result: Lewis reported alpha estimates from 0.90 to 0.96 across tested scenarios.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Use boundary
reliabilityEvidence.result: Three-item alpha is sample/task dependent; report interval/uncertainty and avoid treating high internal consistency as scenario coverage.

validityEvidence.label: Development evidence
validityEvidence.result: The original evaluation reported reliability, sensitivity, and concurrent-validity evidence across three usability tests with eight common scenarios.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: ASQ is a brief subjective post-scenario measure and cannot replace observed success, time, errors, or a broader post-study judgment.

factorEvidence.sample: Three usability tests with eight common scenarios
factorEvidence.result: Three scenario-level items intended for a short overall assessment.
factorEvidence.interpretation: With only three items, inspect item behavior and content coverage rather than over-fitting a complex factor model.

post-study-system-usability-questionnair.summary: Post-study perceived-usability questionnaire with total and System Usefulness, Information Quality, and Interface Quality interpretations.
post-study-system-usability-questionnair.administration: Use the specified PSSUQ version and instructions after representative tasks; document item/version differences and scoring/missing-data rules.
post-study-system-usability-questionnair.licensing: Use the IBM/Lewis source and verify terms for the exact version and reproduction.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Source dataset
reliabilityEvidence.result: Lewis reported total alpha 0.97 and subscale alphas 0.96, 0.91, and 0.91 in the source analyses.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Transfer warning
reliabilityEvidence.result: Very high alpha may reflect item overlap as well as precision. Re-estimate by score and population.

validityEvidence.label: Internal structure
validityEvidence.result: A preliminary 48-person PSSUQ analysis supported three named factors later examined with CSUQ data.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: A general post-study usability score does not test display legibility, workload, flight safety, or mission effectiveness.

factorEvidence.sample: Preliminary PSSUQ factor analysis with 48 participants
factorEvidence.result: System Usefulness, Information Quality, and Interface Quality factors.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Promising original structure with a small preliminary PSSUQ sample; verify the exact version and test the structure in the intended population.

researchNeeds: Factor replication with suitable ordinal estimator

computer-system-usability-questionnaire-.summary: Field-oriented IBM computer-system usability questionnaire related to PSSUQ, with total and three proposed factor scores.
computer-system-usability-questionnaire-.administration: Use the exact CSUQ version, item wording, response scale, and scoring rules; record whether it is being used in field or controlled-test context.
computer-system-usability-questionnaire-.licensing: Use Lewis (1995) and verify terms for the exact instrument version.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Source evidence
reliabilityEvidence.result: Lewis reported internal-consistency evidence for total and three named score families in the IBM questionnaire program.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Context dependency
reliabilityEvidence.result: Estimate reliability for the exact product, population, and administration mode; do not transfer the PSSUQ total coefficient automatically.

validityEvidence.label: Structure and relationship to PSSUQ
validityEvidence.result: A 377-response CSUQ study supported System Usefulness, Information Quality, and Interface Quality groupings.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: Field satisfaction/usability ratings can diverge from observed operational task performance.

factorEvidence.result: System Usefulness, Information Quality, and Interface Quality factors.
factorEvidence.interpretation: More substantial original sample than the preliminary PSSUQ analysis; still test version/language/population transfer.

umux-lite.summary: Two-item perceived usefulness/ease measure designed for situations with severe questionnaire-time limits.
umux-lite.administration: Administer the exact two items and response scale after representative use. Report both items, scoring/transformation, and uncertainty.
umux-lite.licensing: Use Lewis, Utesch, and Maher (2013) and confirm current reuse terms.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Development studies
reliabilityEvidence.result: The two studies reported reliability estimates 0.83 and 0.82.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Two-item rule
reliabilityEvidence.result: Use the inter-item relationship or an appropriate two-item reliability estimate; coefficient alpha is not an informative default for two items.

validityEvidence.label: Convergence with SUS
validityEvidence.result: The two studies reported correlations with SUS of 0.81 and 0.85.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: High correlation with another subjective usability scale does not establish objective efficiency, safety, workload, or legibility.

factorEvidence.estimator: Two-item reliability and relationships with SUS
factorEvidence.result: Usefulness and ease items form a very short global perceived-usability measure.
factorEvidence.interpretation: A two-indicator factor model has limited diagnostic/identification value; prioritize content and external relations.

situation-awareness-rating-technique-sar.summary: Subjective situation-awareness rating technique with 10-dimensional and condensed three-dimensional forms.
situation-awareness-rating-technique-sar.administration: Name the exact SART form and scoring. Administer at a task-appropriate time, retain component ratings, and pair with objective state knowledge and performance.
situation-awareness-rating-technique-sar.licensing: Use the original Taylor source and authorized instrument instructions; do not mix 10D and 3D items/scoring silently.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Scenario dataset
reliabilityEvidence.result: Braarud reported alphas 0.74 and 0.71 for three-item SART at post-session and post-video administrations in the studied control-room setting.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Dependency warning
reliabilityEvidence.result: Those repeated ratings came from 18 operators in six teams across scenarios and should not be treated as a large independent-person sample.

validityEvidence.label: Aircrew development
validityEvidence.result: Taylor developed SART through structured elicitation with 84 RAF test and operational aircrew.

validityEvidence.label: Divergence from SAGAT
validityEvidence.result: SART and SAGAT were not correlated in a display evaluation even though both were sensitive/diagnostic; SART correlated with confidence and subjective performance.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: SART measures perceived situation awareness and can reflect confidence, demand, and performance beliefs. Do not substitute it for state-knowledge accuracy.

factorEvidence.result: Ten dimensions were organized into demand, supply, and understanding groupings.
factorEvidence.interpretation: The 10D and 3D forms are related but distinct implementations; verify the selected scoring model and context.

researchNeeds: Factor replication in intended aviation task

sagat-direct-state-probe-accuracy.summary: Freeze-probe accuracy for current task/environment state, derived from a requirements and goal-directed task analysis.
sagat-direct-state-probe-accuracy.administration: Freeze the simulation at sampled times, blank relevant displays as required, administer predefined state queries, and score responses against synchronized truth.
sagat-direct-state-probe-accuracy.licensing: Use Endsley (1995) and the authorized study protocol; repository does not reproduce a universal item bank because questions must be task-derived.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Scoring reliability
reliabilityEvidence.result: For open or coded responses, establish scorer training and agreement; for objective responses, verify ground-truth synchronization and item difficulty.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Sampling precision
reliabilityEvidence.result: Estimate uncertainty across probes/scenarios and model repeated responses within participant; probes are not independent pilots.

validityEvidence.label: Requirements-derived content
validityEvidence.result: Goal/task analysis and synchronized truth provide the central content/response-process basis for SAGAT queries.

validityEvidence.label: Method comparison
validityEvidence.result: SAGAT and SART were not interchangeable in a direct comparison.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: Poor query content, intrusive freezes, cueing, or unsynchronized truth can invalidate the result even when scoring is objective.

factorEvidence.estimator: Not a generic reflective factor model
factorEvidence.result: Queries sample perception, comprehension, or projection requirements derived from the task.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Do not expect internal consistency among heterogeneous state facts; evaluate content coverage, difficulty, and classification/scoring quality.

sagat-projection-accuracy.summary: Accuracy of freeze-probe predictions about near-future task or system state.
sagat-projection-accuracy.administration: Derive projection questions from task goals, freeze at defensible points, record prediction horizon, and score against synchronized subsequent truth or approved answer logic.
sagat-projection-accuracy.licensing: Use the Endsley SAGAT method and task-specific protocol; no generic projection-item bank is implied.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Scenario sampling
reliabilityEvidence.result: Reliability depends on query sampling, difficulty, prediction horizon, and scoring; report uncertainty and repeated-observation structure.

validityEvidence.label: Construct alignment
validityEvidence.result: Projection probes address future-state knowledge rather than confidence or retrospective workload.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: A forecast may be reasonable yet differ from one stochastic realization. Define allowable answers and time horizon before testing.

factorEvidence.result: Items sample task-specific Level 3 projection requirements.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Use content mapping and item performance; do not force heterogeneous projections into a reflective latent scale without theory.

bedford-workload-rating.summary: Ten-point pilot workload decision-tree rating based on spare mental capacity and task performance.
bedford-workload-rating.administration: Train raters on the exact Bedford decision tree, define the short flight-task segment, collect the decision path/rating immediately after the segment, and retain performance.
bedford-workload-rating.licensing: Use Roscoe and Ellis (1990) or an authorized reproduction of the canonical decision tree.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Repeatability design
reliabilityEvidence.result: Short, well-defined tasks were recommended to improve rating reliability; report rater/pilot training and task segmentation.
reliabilityEvidence.source: Roscoe & Ellis (1990); FAA DOT/FAA/CT-TN95/49 Appendix A

reliabilityEvidence.label: Ordinal agreement
reliabilityEvidence.result: For multiple raters or repeat conditions, use an ordinal agreement/repeatability approach and preserve decision paths.

validityEvidence.label: Aviation construct fit
validityEvidence.result: The method was developed for pilot spare-capacity/workload judgments and has extensive flight use described by its authors.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: Bedford is subjective and task-specific. It does not replace achieved performance, error, safety-margin, or physiological evidence.

factorEvidence.result: Decision path yields one ordinal workload category/rating.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Factor analysis and alpha are not applicable; evaluate rater training, repeatability, sensitivity, and task linkage.

cooper-harper-handling-qualities-rating.summary: Ordinal pilot rating of handling qualities and required compensation for a specified task, configuration, and performance criteria.
cooper-harper-handling-qualities-rating.administration: Before the run, define desired and adequate task performance. Train the pilot on the decision tree; collect rating, branch decisions, comments, compensation, task performance, and vehicle/configuration state.
cooper-harper-handling-qualities-rating.licensing: Use Cooper and Harper (1969) or an authorized canonical scale reproduction; do not rewrite anchors and still call it Cooper–Harper.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Repeatability/agreement
reliabilityEvidence.result: Analyze ordinal within-pilot repeatability and between-pilot agreement while retaining task performance and configuration. Correlation alone is not agreement.

reliabilityEvidence.label: No internal consistency
reliabilityEvidence.result: This is a single decision-tree outcome; alpha and item-factor analysis are not applicable.

validityEvidence.label: Task-performance anchoring
validityEvidence.result: The decision tree explicitly links handling difficulty and pilot compensation to desired/adequate task performance.

validityEvidence.label: Application review
validityEvidence.result: NASA review emphasizes absolute, ordinal, task/configuration-specific interpretation with comments and performance.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: Do not use Cooper–Harper as a generic workload, usability, preference, or comfort score.
validityEvidence.source: FAA HF Version 3.0; Bailey et al. (2009)

factorEvidence.result: One rating derived from task performance, handling difficulty, and required pilot compensation.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Validity rests on task criteria, decision path, trained pilot judgment, and achieved performance—not item loadings.

subjective-workload-assessment-technique.summary: Subjective workload technique covering time load, mental effort load, and psychological stress load with a defined scaling/scoring procedure.
subjective-workload-assessment-technique.administration: Use the selected SWAT version, conduct the prescribed scale-development/card-sort procedure or justified group solution, collect event ratings, and record scoring method.
subjective-workload-assessment-technique.licensing: Use the public SWAT Version 3.1 guide and original development sources; verify current reproduction terms.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Scaling stability
reliabilityEvidence.result: Report the individual/group scaling solution and evaluate stability/sensitivity across comparable events; do not substitute generic alpha for the conjoint measurement procedure.

validityEvidence.label: Development evidence
validityEvidence.result: Early work reported construct and concurrent-validity tests using conjoint measurement.

validityEvidence.label: Comparative evidence
validityEvidence.result: TLX and SWAT had equivalent sensitivity in one manipulated tracking experiment, but differ in psychometric structure.

validityEvidence.label: limitation
validityEvidence.result: The three dimensions and scaling solution are not interchangeable with TLX subscales or an arbitrary average.

factorEvidence.estimator: Conjoint scaling rather than a generic reflective CFA
factorEvidence.result: Time load, mental effort load, and psychological stress load are combined using a defined scaling solution.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Preserve the scaling model; a post hoc factor model is not a substitute for SWAT administration/scoring.

instantaneous-self-assessment-isa.summary: Brief repeated rating intended to track momentary workload during a real-time task.
instantaneous-self-assessment-isa.administration: Use the defined five-level scale/anchors and prompt schedule; synchronize prompts/responses to task events and record response modality, missed prompts, and local performance around each prompt.
instantaneous-self-assessment-isa.licensing: Use the EUROCONTROL ERGO documentation and exact chosen implementation.

reliabilityEvidence.label: Repeated-measures precision
reliabilityEvidence.result: Model ratings as repeated within-person observations, estimate condition/time sensitivity, and report missing prompts. Do not treat prompts as independent participants.

validityEvidence.label: Relations and sensitivity
validityEvidence.result: ISA was sensitive to task difficulty and correlated with several post-task, heart-rate, and performance comparators in an experimental evaluation.

validityEvidence.label: Prompt reactivity
validityEvidence.result: Primary tracking performance worsened when a manual or spoken ISA response was required.

validityEvidence.label: Temporal distinction
validityEvidence.result: EUROCONTROL studies kept repeated ISA separate from post-exercise NASA-TLX, supporting different temporal interpretations.

factorEvidence.result: One momentary ordinal workload response per prompt.
factorEvidence.interpretation: Factor analysis and alpha are not applicable. Evaluate reactivity, ordinal repeatability, sensitivity, timing, and missingness.

verificationPathways.label: Display / alerting
verificationPathways.title: Flight-deck display legibility and visual alerting
verificationPathways.question: Can the intended pilot detect, identify, understand, and correctly act on a configured visual alert while preserving the primary flight task?
verificationPathways.summary: A layered verification case joining calibrated display measurements with representative-user alert performance under daylight, night, NVIS, optical-gear, concurrency, and cascading-failure conditions.
verificationPathways.claim: The configured presentation is physically viewable and supports correct detect–identify–act performance within program-approved operational constraints.
verificationPathways.scenario: A pilot maintaining a primary flight task receives a warning, caution, or advisory alone or during a cascading failure under a specified daylight, night, or NVIS condition.
verificationPathways.task: Detect the alert, discriminate priority, identify the condition, select the correct response, and preserve higher-priority aircraft control.
failureMechanisms: Attentional capture that degrades the primary flight task

evidenceGroups.purpose: Score detection, correct interpretation, and action against independent injected-state truth and an approved response rubric.
Test the applicable physical criteria with calibrated equipment, documented geometry, ambient condition, and uncertainty.
Expose tradeoffs so faster alert response cannot hide degraded aircraft control or critical omissions.
Characterize perceived workload and visual search without substituting either for correct task performance.

conditions: Full-sun/daylight context and installed lighting extremes where applicable
Night/dark and applicable NVIS configuration
Design eye plus required viewing-envelope positions
Operational helmets and clear/tinted visors or other optical gear
Nominal, competing, and representative cascading alerts
Primary-task concurrency and production-representative software/symbology
artifacts: Applicable requirement and tailoring/certification-basis extract
Test card, event truth, response rubric, and critical-failure rules
Display, lighting, eye-point, visor, and software configuration record
Instrument calibration, geometry diagram, raw photometry, and uncertainty
Time-synchronized event, flight/control, observer, and response data
Participant/gear coverage, deviations, discrepancies, and authority disposition
decisionRules: Keep physical-criterion and human-task findings separate.
Predeclare critical misses and wrong actions; do not average them away.
Use task- or hazard-derived timing limits approved by the program.
Treat workload, gaze, confidence, and preference as diagnostic evidence.
boundaries: System safety or certification from photometry alone
Compliance with MIL-HDBK-516D, which is guidance
Transfer of a workload score into an objective performance finding

sources.label: FAA flight-deck human-factors report
sources.locator: Version 3.0, Appendix B and Appendix C.1/C.6

verificationPathways.label: HUD / HMD
verificationPathways.title: HUD/HMD optical, tracking, and operational integration
verificationPathways.question: Does the configured optical path, imagery, tracker, helmet integration, and timing support the specified outside-view task across the approved user and operating envelope?
verificationPathways.summary: A progressive bench-to-HITL pathway that keeps optical/engineering conformance, task performance, human integration, and symptom evidence in their correct roles.
verificationPathways.claim: The configured HUD/HMD supports the specified outside-view and aircraft-control tasks across approved eye/head pose, gear, light, maneuver, and display states.
verificationPathways.scenario: During taxi, takeoff, maneuvering, approach, or landing, the pilot acquires and interprets referenced information while preserving outside-world visibility, flight-path control, and hazard detection.
verificationPathways.task: Acquire, align, interpret, and act on displayed and outside-world information through head movement, lighting changes, and representative aircraft dynamics.
failureMechanisms: Occlusion or loss of task-critical field
Misregistration, parallax, boresight error, or drift
Lag, jitter, or double imagery during motion
Restricted head movement, unstable fit, discomfort, or disorientation

evidenceGroups.purpose: Evaluate correct symbol interpretation, target/hazard response, task completion, and aircraft-control outcomes against task-specific truth and tolerances.
Map performance across the required field, eye/head pose, display mode, lighting, and installed alignment state.
Test fit, alignment, stability, visibility, mobility, and physical loading for the specified population, gear, and duration.
Characterize symptoms, burden, and perceived workload without using them as substitutes for optical or task criteria.

conditions: Required day, night, NVD/NVIS, and transition lighting states
Eye box, exit pupil, eye relief, field angle, and representative head poses
Helmet/HMD size, visor, eyewear, mask, and other operational gear
Static and dynamic alignment, thermal/mechanical state, vibration, and maneuver
Normal, degraded, declutter, tracker-loss, and recovery states
Progression from calibrated bench and HITL to ground/flight only when authorized
artifacts: Applicable criteria, task-region analysis, and approved operational claim
Optical-bench configuration, calibration, reference geometry, and uncertainty
Field/eye/head-pose maps for FOV, registration, latency, jitter, and occlusion
Helmet/gear fit, mass/CG, mobility, and participant accommodation records
Time-synchronized task, flight/control, tracker, display, and adverse-event data
Stage-transfer argument, limitations, discrepancies, and authority disposition
decisionRules: Give each optical or timing criterion its own visible result.
Require task-level evidence for operational use, not bench conformance alone.
Treat symptoms and comfort as risk/diagnostic evidence, not proof of task support.
State what transfers between bench, simulator, aircraft ground, and flight—and why.
boundaries: Operational integration from optical-bench data alone
Universal latency, registration, comfort, or workload thresholds
Flight suitability from one helmet size, eye point, or lighting condition
Use of TBD MIL-HDBK-87213B HMD sections as completed test methods

sources.label: MIL-HDBK-87213B official record
sources.locator: §§4.2.1.25–4.2.1.26; note unresolved TBD HMD verification text

verificationPathways.label: Workload / handling
verificationPathways.title: Mode management, workload, and handling qualities
verificationPathways.question: Can a qualified pilot correctly manage and recover the system state while maintaining approved flight-task performance and an authority-accepted workload/handling-qualities basis?
verificationPathways.summary: A synthetic mode-transition pathway that prevents subjective workload or a handling rating from hiding state confusion, unsafe commands, failed recovery, or loss of aircraft control.
verificationPathways.claim: The pilot can distinguish, command, verify, and recover the specified mode states while maintaining approved flight/control performance in nominal, concurrent, degraded, and failure conditions.
verificationPathways.scenario: A requested mode transition is activated, deferred, rejected, or degraded while the pilot maintains a primary flight task and a representative communication or monitoring task.
verificationPathways.task: Assess the current and requested state, command if needed, verify achieved state, recover from unexpected behavior, and preserve aircraft control.
failureMechanisms: Fixation, flight-path excursion, or loss of performance reserve

evidenceGroups.purpose: Score mode-state understanding, command/recovery correctness, critical errors, and primary flight performance against independent system truth.
Reveal control effort, reversals, communication cost, and response timing that explain performance reserve and failure mechanisms.
Describe subjective demand, spare capacity, and perceived state awareness with the exact version, timing, and scoring preserved.
Use the original decision-tree construct only after desired and adequate performance are defined for the exact task and configuration.

conditions: Activated, deferred, rejected/inhibited, and failed transition outcomes
Nominal, high-concurrency, degraded, and recovery scenarios
Representative primary flight plus communication/monitoring demand
Qualified pilot population, familiarization, and stable proficiency
Applicable flight phases, loadings, configurations, and environments
High-fidelity simulator with independent selected/accepted/active/achieved state logs
artifacts: Functional/task analysis, state model, hazard link, and operational claim
Desired/adequate performance definitions and acceptance authority
Simulator model/fidelity statement, crew qualification, and familiarization record
Scenario scripts and independent state, event, aircraft, and control logs
Observer/error adjudication plus exact rating-scale instructions and timing
Tradeoff analysis, uncertainty, deviations, discrepancies, and authority disposition
decisionRules: Keep every critical error and loss-of-control event visible.
Do not interpret “no significant difference” as equivalence.
Define the exact role of workload and handling ratings before data collection.
Preserve ordinal decision paths, achieved performance, and pilot comments.
boundaries: Adequate performance, safety, or airworthiness from TLX/Bedford alone
General usability or workload from Cooper–Harper
A public clause mapping to controlled MIL-STD-1797B text
Automatic transfer from simulator to flight

verificationPathways.label: Pilot ergonomics
verificationPathways.title: Pilot accommodation, reach, visibility, and ergonomics
verificationPathways.question: Can the approved target pilot population, clothed, equipped, and restrained as required, see, reach, fully actuate, and safely use the applicable controls and displays?
verificationPathways.summary: A multivariate accommodation pathway that joins population-boundary analysis, installed geometry, control force/travel, visibility, and representative task demonstration.
verificationPathways.claim: The specified multivariate pilot population can safely complete the required normal, emergency, and recovery tasks across applicable station settings and operational equipment.
verificationPathways.scenario: Multivariate accommodation-envelope boundary cases perform normal control/display tasks and an emergency or recovery sequence at applicable seat/restraint positions with operational gear.
verificationPathways.task: View, identify, reach, grasp, fully actuate, verify, release/recover, and egress where applicable without obstruction, excessive force, or unsafe posture.
failureMechanisms: Obstructed control, display, or outside-world view
Excessive reach, force, posture, or contact loading
Restricted motion, incomplete control travel, or inadvertent actuation
Helmet/equipment interference or inability to execute an emergency action

evidenceGroups.purpose: Demonstrate complete, correct, and safe operation of every required task/control across approved boundary cases and station settings.
Quantify joint population coverage, reach, clearance, and control access using the approved anthropometric database and multivariate method.
Expose fit, head/limb movement, equipment mass/CG, visibility, and installed interference in the actual task and gear configuration.
Record exertion, discomfort, and symptoms as supporting burden evidence with predefined stop criteria.

conditions: Approved male/female multivariate boundary cases, not independent percentile mannequins
Operational clothing, helmet/HMD, visor, mask, gloves, footwear, and protective/survival gear
Extreme and intermediate seat positions plus operational restraint states
Normal, degraded, emergency, recovery, and applicable egress tasks
Full control travel, required force, repeated/continuous action, and both hands where required
Production-representative geometry with adjacent equipment, cables, and installed obstructions
artifacts: Target-population definition, database/version, dimensions, and multivariate method
Boundary-case derivation and digital-model assumptions/validation
Participant body measurements, gear sizes, seat/restraint settings, and configuration survey
Reach, clearance, force, travel, FOV, task, error, and safety-monitoring records
Uncovered population estimate, limitations, exceptions, and accepted omissions
Discrepancies, corrective actions, retest need, and authority disposition
decisionRules: Use the invoked population criterion and approved target population.
Evaluate joint task success; never add marginal percentile coverages.
Confirm consequential model results with representative hardware and users.
Keep comfort/exertion separate from reach, clearance, visibility, and control authority.
boundaries: Multivariate accommodation from a fifth-percentile female and 95th-percentile male alone
Task operability from a digital human model alone
Safe reach, visibility, or egress from comfort ratings
Universal use of the 90/95/99-percent values outside the invoked and tailored context

sources.label: MIL-STD-46855A official record
sources.locator: §§5.3–5.3.3; representative users, conditions, discrepancies, and errors

psychometricConcepts.name: Intended interpretation and use
psychometricConcepts.question: What claim and decision will this score support?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Validity concerns evidence and theory supporting an interpretation of scores for a specified use—not a permanent property or a single coefficient.
psychometricConcepts.use: Before selecting a measure, write the construct, population, task, score meaning, decision, and cost of error.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Calling an instrument “validated” without naming version, population, context, interpretation, or decision.
psychometricConcepts.record: Construct; score; population; task/context; decision; consequences; required evidence.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Content evidence
psychometricConcepts.question: Do items and tasks cover the intended construct and operational domain?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Evidence from a documented domain, task analysis, expert judgment, and coverage of relevant facets and failure/degraded states.
psychometricConcepts.use: When building or adapting items, scenarios, probes, checklists, or performance rubrics.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Treating a generic usability total as complete coverage of fighter flight-deck usability or mission safety.
psychometricConcepts.record: Domain map; task/goal analysis; expert selection; missing-domain review; item-to-construct trace.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Response-process evidence
psychometricConcepts.question: Are people or raters using the intended judgment process?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Evidence that respondents understand items, use expected cues, and apply scoring/rating rules as intended.
psychometricConcepts.use: For new wording, specialized populations, translations, expert ratings, and scenario probes.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Assuming pilots interpret “performance” as self-performance when they may think it means aircraft performance.
psychometricConcepts.record: Cognitive interviews; think-aloud/debrief; rater training; comprehension probes; response timing; missingness.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Internal-structure evidence
psychometricConcepts.question: Do item relations support the proposed score and dimensionality?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Evidence from dimensionality, factor structure, residuals, local dependence, item functioning, and reliability conditional on the model.
psychometricConcepts.use: Before reporting questionnaire totals/subscales or comparing latent constructs.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Using alpha as proof of one factor, or selecting a model only because one fit index crosses a rule of thumb.
psychometricConcepts.record: Model; estimator; item treatment; sample; loadings/cross-loadings; residuals; fit; competing models; uncertainty.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Relations to other variables
psychometricConcepts.question: Are prespecified convergent, discriminant, criterion, and known-groups relations observed?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Evidence that scores relate—and do not relate—to external measures in ways predicted by the construct and decision model.
psychometricConcepts.use: To distinguish workload from usability, confidence from state knowledge, and preference from performance.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Treating correlation with another self-report as proof of objective operational performance or causal validity.
psychometricConcepts.record: A priori hypotheses; comparator quality; timing; effect and interval; multiplicity; alternative explanations.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Consequences and decision accuracy
psychometricConcepts.question: What errors or harms follow from using this score or cutoff?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Evidence about intended/unintended consequences, classification errors, subgroup impacts, and decision costs.
psychometricConcepts.use: Whenever a score triggers acceptance, training, redesign, selection, or safety action.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Turning a sample percentile or handbook example into a certification threshold without authority.
psychometricConcepts.record: Decision rule; authority; false-positive/false-negative costs; subgroup performance; appeals/discrepancy handling.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Internal consistency (alpha / omega)
psychometricConcepts.question: Do reflective items cohere at one occasion under a defensible dimensional model?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Alpha and model-based omega summarize score dependability due to item sampling under different assumptions.
psychometricConcepts.use: For multi-item reflective scores after dimensionality and item coding are checked.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Using alpha for single items, formative indexes, heterogeneous checklists, or as proof of validity/unidimensionality.
psychometricConcepts.record: Coefficient and interval; alpha/omega variant; model; item set/coding; sample; missing data; dimensionality.

psychometricConcepts.name: Test–retest stability
psychometricConcepts.question: Are scores stable over an interval when the construct should be stable?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Agreement/stability of repeated measurements across an interval with no expected true change.
psychometricConcepts.use: For traits or stable system judgments and for evaluating score repeatability under matched conditions.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Demanding high stability for workload that should change with task demand, learning, fatigue, or system state.
psychometricConcepts.record: Interval; intervening events; stability assumption; correlation and agreement/ICC; paired change; confidence interval.

psychometricConcepts.name: Inter-rater agreement
psychometricConcepts.question: Would trained raters assign the same codes or scores?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Agreement beyond chance for categorical/ordinal codes or consistency/agreement for continuous ratings.
psychometricConcepts.use: For observer error codes, posture scores, workload/handling ratings, and qualitative classifications.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Reporting a Pearson correlation as agreement or omitting the kappa/ICC variant and rater protocol.
psychometricConcepts.record: Raters; training; independence; prevalence; unit; statistic/variant; interval; adjudication.

psychometricConcepts.name: Measurement error and SEM
psychometricConcepts.question: How uncertain is an individual score or change?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Standard error of measurement/change or a model-based posterior interval quantifies score uncertainty under the stated design.
psychometricConcepts.use: For individual interpretation, change classification, pass/fail decisions, and sensor/instrument results.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Using a group reliability coefficient as if every score has equal precision, or treating a tiny change as real.
psychometricConcepts.record: Error source/model; SEM or conditional interval; confidence level; repeatability; calibration/uncertainty budget.

psychometricConcepts.name: Exploratory factor analysis (EFA)
psychometricConcepts.question: What plausible latent structure is present when structure is uncertain?
psychometricConcepts.definition: EFA estimates common-factor structure while allowing items to load on multiple factors; it is not the same as principal-components analysis.
psychometricConcepts.use: During scale development or when theory and prior structures do not fit the target population/version.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Using PCA as latent-factor proof, defaulting to eigenvalues greater than one, or suppressing meaningful cross-loadings.
psychometricConcepts.record: Correlation type; estimator; factor-retention evidence; oblique rotation; loadings; cross-loadings; communalities; residuals.

psychometricConcepts.name: Factor retention / parallel analysis
psychometricConcepts.question: How many factors are supported beyond sampling noise?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Parallel analysis compares observed eigenvalues with eigenvalues from random data and is one input to factor-retention decisions.
psychometricConcepts.use: With theory, scree, interpretability, residuals, and competing models during EFA.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Treating parallel analysis or any one rule as an automatic answer detached from theory and data quality.
psychometricConcepts.record: Simulation method; percentile; sample/item count; observed/random eigenvalues; competing factor counts.

psychometricConcepts.name: Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)
psychometricConcepts.question: Does a prespecified measurement model reproduce the item relationships adequately?
psychometricConcepts.definition: CFA tests a theory-specified loading, factor, residual, and covariance structure using an estimator suited to the data.
psychometricConcepts.use: For score/subscore confirmation, competing models, invariance, and latent relations.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Modifying until fit appears acceptable, using an unsuitable estimator for ordinal items, or treating rule-of-thumb cutoffs as universal laws.
psychometricConcepts.record: Model syntax; estimator; item scale; identification; sample; loadings; residuals; fit indices with intervals; modifications and rationale.

psychometricConcepts.name: Fit indices and cutoffs
psychometricConcepts.question: How well does the model reproduce the observed relationships, and where does it fail?
psychometricConcepts.definition: CFI/TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, residuals, and model comparisons summarize different aspects of fit and are sensitive to model/data conditions.
psychometricConcepts.use: Together with substantive theory, parameter plausibility, residual diagnostics, and competing models.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Declaring validity because CFI or RMSEA crosses a popular cutoff without examining misspecification.
psychometricConcepts.record: All prespecified fit indices; uncertainty; test statistic/df; residuals; sample/model conditions; comparison rationale.

psychometricConcepts.name: Item loadings and cross-loadings
psychometricConcepts.question: How strongly and uniquely does each item relate to the proposed factor?
psychometricConcepts.definition: A loading is a study/model-specific relation between an item and factor; cross-loadings and residuals show ambiguity or local mismatch.
psychometricConcepts.use: To evaluate score meaning, weak/redundant items, cross-construct contamination, and stability across groups.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Applying universal loading cutoffs or deleting items solely to maximize fit without content consequences.
psychometricConcepts.record: Every item; factor; standardized/unstandardized loading; SE/interval; cross-loadings; residual variance; wording/coding.

psychometricConcepts.name: Measurement invariance
psychometricConcepts.question: Do scores mean the same thing across groups, languages, equipment, or time?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Configural, metric, scalar, and residual invariance examine whether factor form, loadings, thresholds/intercepts, and residuals are comparable.
psychometricConcepts.use: Before comparing means or trends across pilot groups, languages, versions, systems, or repeated occasions.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Comparing group means after establishing only similar-looking factors or pooled reliability.
psychometricConcepts.record: Groups/times; model sequence; estimator; parameter constraints; fit changes; partial invariance; impact on comparisons.

psychometricConcepts.name: Differential item functioning (DIF)
psychometricConcepts.question: Do equally positioned people from different groups respond differently to an item?
psychometricConcepts.definition: DIF evaluates group-related item behavior after conditioning on the measured construct.
psychometricConcepts.use: For fairness, translations, expertise groups, equipment configurations, or response-mode differences.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Calling any group item-mean difference DIF without conditioning on the construct, or removing items without content analysis.
psychometricConcepts.record: Grouping variable; conditioning model; DIF method; effect size; uncertainty; item content review; impact on scores.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)

psychometricConcepts.name: Item response theory / information
psychometricConcepts.question: Where along the construct is each item and the total score precise?
psychometricConcepts.definition: IRT models item response as a function of a latent trait; graded-response models are one option for ordered questionnaire items.
psychometricConcepts.use: For conditional precision, item banks, adaptive testing, category functioning, and DIF when sample/design support it.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Fitting a complex IRT model to a small convenience sample or ignoring dimensionality and local independence.
psychometricConcepts.record: Model; link; category curves; discrimination/thresholds; information; local dependence; fit; sample; scoring scale.

psychometricConcepts.name: Sensitivity and responsiveness
psychometricConcepts.question: Can the measure detect the intended condition difference or meaningful change?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Sensitivity concerns detecting differences; responsiveness concerns change over time relative to true change and measurement error.
psychometricConcepts.use: For interface comparisons, training effects, fatigue progression, and intervention evaluation.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Equating statistical significance with operational importance or using reliability as proof of responsiveness.
psychometricConcepts.record: Expected direction/magnitude; anchor; effect and interval; measurement error; floor/ceiling; multiplicity; task condition.

psychometricConcepts.name: Floor and ceiling effects
psychometricConcepts.question: Does the score have room to distinguish poor/good performance or change?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Concentration at scale bounds limits discrimination, change detection, and sometimes factor/correlation estimates.
psychometricConcepts.use: During pilot testing and before relying on a score in expert or highly constrained samples.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Concluding all systems or pilots are equivalent when an easy task or coarse scale compresses scores at a boundary.
psychometricConcepts.record: Proportion at each bound; item distributions; subgroup/condition breakdown; task difficulty; missingness.

psychometricConcepts.name: Classification and threshold uncertainty
psychometricConcepts.question: How often could measurement uncertainty change the decision?
psychometricConcepts.definition: Decision accuracy depends on score uncertainty, threshold authority, base rates, and the relative cost of false passes and failures.
psychometricConcepts.use: For requirements verification, screening, acceptance, and hazard-linked decisions.
psychometricConcepts.misuse: Applying a sample-derived “good/bad” label as a universal pass/fail threshold.
psychometricConcepts.record: Threshold source/authority; uncertainty; sensitivity/specificity if applicable; base rate; error costs; borderline rule.
psychometricConcepts.source: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014)
